rv.q: The performances are glorious, too: Miya James is both unshowy and mesmeric as Raelynn; Saltburn’s Sadie Soverall is horribly compelling as the wild and glowering Shelby.

And what a joyous, blazingly intelligent play this is: at once a restless interrogation of the role of art in defining and expressing who we are; a compassionate, funny portrayal of what it means to be a teenage girl; and a furious appraisal of the way power games repeat across generations.
In a drama that exists between extremes of ignorance and self-knowledge, the brilliant tension is that those girls, who have so much more to learn, are showing us the way.

John Proctor Is The Villain is a buzzing show about a bunch of American teenagers, mostly girls, in Georgia in 2018. The title refers to the dubious hero of Arthur Miller’s The Crucible. The male teacher (Donal Finn) is a woke goody- two-shoes, but you start to wonder if he is all he seems.

Kimberly Belflower’s hit Broadway play John Proctor is the Villain (getting its UK premiere at the Royal Court) is a fantastically cathartic riff on Arthur Miller’s witch-trial play The Crucible, one that captures the enraging reality of high school life at the peak of the #MeToo movement in 2018.

Danya Taymor’s production – which transfers recast from a smash Broadway run – is an absolute blast, the many serious issues raised all of a piece with its breathless ebullience and Belflower’s endlessly witty text.
And on victim-blaming and the excuses people make for predators.
Belflower’s play is, in many ways, one familiar story wrapped in another; but it’s done with wit and leaves us, with its final, glorious act of rebellion, on a high of irrepressible optimism.

There’s certainly plenty to savour in Danya Taymor’s high-energy production, recast for London audiences, which burrows deep inside the overheated psyches of teenagers. At its sharpest, the dialogue generates waves of laughter too. … Belflower can’t quite resist forcing home her message in the closing scenes.
It is a moving play all the same, and catches the mood of 2018 for a bewildered generation of girls growing into womanhood in the shadow of Weinstein.
This play likewise makes me want to scream, laugh, cry, and dance.
It’s socially engaged contemporary theatre at its best.
One can only hope that the vital and compelling John Proctor is the Villain takes its place beside it in the curriculum.
It also makes for a fascinating and thoroughly entertaining evening of theatre and I would encourage everyone to try and secure a ticket.

A strong and sophisticated script with a committed and convincing cast is rather let down by a sluggish production, and patience is only somewhat rewarded by the time the curtain call finally comes round.
Rarely have I seen a piece with so much depth to it - no reference, however seemingly inconsequential, is there without reason, each serving a key purpose.
John Proctor is the Villain is a moving, heartfelt, and hilarious piece of theatre that spills over the boundaries of make believe and into the complex real life of what it means to be human.
This play risks being cringeworthy; if it means young girls can feel heard, it feels very powerful.
Bright, vital and enchanting, John Proctor is the Villain tackles difficult themes and situations with cautious humour, running at a breakneck speed across 1 hour and 45 minutes.
It is just such a tender piece of work.
John Proctor is the Villain is a triumph of a production, relatable yet sufficiently dramatic.
The apotheosis is both thrilling and more than timely.
The magnificent cast builds up a group energy for a finale that will not be forgotten...
This is the type of play that makes people fall in love with theatre, and it’s a perfect fit for the Royal Court Theatre.
It is a four star triumph that respects its characters’ humanity while fiercely questioning the status quo.
John Proctor is the Villain takes a classic text and spins it on its head.

John Proctor is the Villain is a script to be pored over, studied in much the same way the group of Georgia school students analyse Arthur Miller’s The Crucible in Kimberly Belflower’s seven-time Tony Award-nominated play.

Taymor, who has already directed the play in the US, has drawn strong performances from her British cast and her sympathetic production of Belflower’s play will undoubtedly press many buttons with a young female audience, just as it has done in the States.
Danya Taymor’s direction is perceptive and, as the tension builds, the cast are electric – especially Soverall and James.
You want to cackle and dance and cry with these witches.

The performances are all outstanding, and the teenage friendships are played with relatable tenderness and hilarity, with numerous laugh-out-loud moments throughout an uninterrupted one hour 50 runtime.
It is unsettling and thought-provoking without ever feeling preachy, and is ultimately quite moving.

Although the plot is absorbing and the writing displays deftness, its embryonic dramaturgy makes it a passable but not remarkable experience at the theatre — and in no way matches the excellence of Miller's enduring work.

cn.t: Critics hail Belflower's provocative interrogation of *The Crucible* as blazingly intelligent and deeply moving, with particular praise for its authentic teenage voices and #MeToo resonance, though some find it overly explicit or slow to gather power.

vr.q: You have to go and see this play if you can, especially if you're a young woman, especially if you're someone to whom these themes will be relevant and personal.
